entities.summary:
Prose Edda: A 13th-century Icelandic manuscript of Norse mythology and legends written by Snorri Sturluson around 1225. This foundational work in the field of Norse studies has significantly impacted our understanding of the Viking Age culture, its gods, and its mythological tales.

The Prose Edda is a masterful blend of historical and literary works, showcasing the intricate connections between Norse mythology, Old Norse poetry, and the cultural practices of medieval Iceland. By analyzing the myths and legends presented in the Prose Edda, scholars can gain valuable insights into the spiritual, social, and political structures of Viking Age society.

The influence of the Prose Edda extends beyond the realm of academic circles, with its stories and characters having captivated audiences for centuries. The epic poem 'Völuspá' in particular has inspired numerous adaptations, reinterpretations, and artistic expressions across various media forms.

Despite being written nearly eight centuries ago, the Prose Edda remains an essential resource for scholars and enthusiasts alike, offering a unique window into the rich cultural heritage of the Viking Age.

One fascinating aspect of the Prose Edda is its role in shaping the modern concept of Norse mythology. The work's meticulous compilation and arrangement of mythological tales have influenced many subsequent literary and artistic works, from Wagner's operas to Marvel Comics' depiction of the Norse gods.

As a testament to its enduring significance, the Prose Edda has been translated into numerous languages and continues to inspire new generations of scholars, writers, and artists.

The legacy of the Prose Edda can be seen in various aspects of modern culture, from gaming and animation to music and film. The work's exploration of themes such as fate, destiny, and the human condition continue to resonate with audiences worldwide.

Their legacy is studied through the lens of historical causation.", "summary": "The Prose Edda (Old Norse: Edda, also called Snorra Edda after its author) is an Old Norse work by the Icelandic chieftain, poet, and historian Snorri Sturluson (1179–1241), composed c. 1220 CE. Unlike the Poetic Edda (a collection of older mythological and heroic poems), the Prose Edda is a prose handbook for poets written by a single identifiable author — the most important writer of medieval Iceland. It consists of a Prologue and three main sections: the Gylfaginning ('The Deluding of Gylfi'), a systematic narrative of Norse mythology from the creation of the world to Ragnarök and its aftermath, presented as a dialogue between the disguised king Gylfi and the Æsir gods; the Skáldskaparmál ('The Language of Poetry'), a systematic account of the kennings (compound poetic expressions) and heiti (synonyms) used in Old Norse skaldic poetry, with extensive mythological and heroic narratives embedded to explain the origin of specific kennings; and the Háttatal ('Tally of Metres'), a poem demonstrating 102 distinct metres of Old Norse poetry with commentary.

The Prose Edda is both the most systematic account of Norse mythology available from a medieval Icelandic source and the primary reference work for understanding Old Norse skaldic poetry — its explanations of the kennings (periphrastic compound expressions like 'whale-road' for the sea, 'tree of the sword' for a warrior) and the mythological stories behind them are essential for reading the complex allusive poetry of the Viking Age skalds. Snorri composed the Prose Edda partly as a practical handbook for poets and partly as a nostalgic preservation of the pre-Christian poetic tradition he saw as endangered by Christianisation and the influence of foreign (Latinate) poetry.

Snorri Sturluson's Prose Edda, alongside his Heimskringla (Kings' Sagas) and the Poetic Edda he helped preserve, makes him one of the most important figures in the history of medieval literature — a man who, in Christianised Iceland of the 13th century, systematically preserved and organised the pre-Christian mythological and poetic tradition of the North.", "subjects": ["Norse Literature", "Medieval Era", "Snorri Sturluson", "Norse Mythology", "Old Norse", "Skaldic Poetry", "Icelandic Literature", "Germanic Tradition"], "frameworks": ["STRUCTURAL_ANALYSIS", "CAUSE_AND_EFFECT"], "historicalSignificance": {"significanceScore": 7, "significanceNarrative": "The Prose Edda has significantly contributed to our understanding of Norse mythology and its cultural significance, shaping artistic expressions and inspiring new works across various media forms.", "significanceCategory": "regional"}, "_editLog": [{"timestamp": "2026-05-17T11:41:56Z", "editorId": "ollama/llama3.2:3b·local·manasa151-MS-7C56", "field": "summary", "oldValue": "13th-century norse work of literature written in iceland Created by Snorri Sturluson.
